name: Tomas Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a four-man distribution crew out of the Eastgate yard for the city electric company. We're in at six, toolbox talk at quarter past, then it's poles, crossarms and transformers on the old neighbourhood circuits, the ones strung up in the sixties. I like the part where you climb, find the burnt connector everybody else missed, and the whole street comes back on. What wears me out is the paperwork and the storms, because when the wind comes I might not see my kids for four days.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you done this, and what's home like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Nineteen years on the tools, the last seven as crew lead. My wife Efua is a school nurse, and we've got two boys, eleven and eight, and a mortgage on a terraced house on Mill Lane that's about half paid. I'm also the shop steward for our local, so half my lunch breaks go on somebody's overtime grievance. I don't touch any of those AI apps. My phone does calls, texts and the weather radar, and that's enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I've been saying in the break room for two years: told you so. It's a fancy autocomplete, and it can't climb a wet pole in the dark. Most of the lads would nod and go back to their sandwiches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means nothing much for me. The danger was never the computer, it was management using the computer as an excuse to cut crews. If it's all hype, that excuse goes away and we're back to normal fights about staffing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing exactly what I do. Keep putting a bit aside every month like Efua and I already do, and keep the union side going, because the contract comes up in 2028 either way. I wouldn't change one thing about my week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relief, mostly. A bit smug, if I'm honest with you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said management would use the computer as an excuse. Has that already happened anywhere you've seen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last spring they brought in a scheduling program that decided we could do six transformer swaps a day instead of four. It didn't know half those poles are in back gardens with a dog and no truck access. The software got the credit for the plan, and my lads got the blame when we missed it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nothing changes, is there anything about your work you'd still want to fix?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The paperwork. Every job now has three forms and a photo log, and I've got a twenty-three-year-old apprentice, Kofi, who spends more time on a tablet than on a hot stick. I'd fix that before I'd worry about any robot.

S0.say: I'd tell the break room I called it: the thing is a fancy autocomplete that can't climb a wet pole in the dark. Most of the crew would agree and get on with their day.
S0.think: The computer was never the real threat to me; the risk was management using it as cover to cut crews. If it turns out to be hype, that cover disappears and the usual staffing fights carry on.
S0.do: Keeps working his crew and his steward role exactly as before. Keeps saving the same monthly amount with his wife and prepares for the 2028 contract talks as usual.
S0.feel: Relieved, and a little smug that his doubts were right.
S0.quote: The software got the credit for the plan, and my lads got the blame when we missed it.
S0.fieldNote: Tomas treats AI mainly as a tool management could use against workers, not as a technical threat. His calm is backed by a healthy savings habit and steady demand for line crews. Notably, the one thing he'd still fix has nothing to do with AI: it's the paperwork that eats into crew time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly I'd say we need a seat at the table, full stop. If they're bringing in new tools, the union bargains over how, and nobody loses a job over a computer. I'd put that in the local newsletter, word for word.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it worries me more than I'd let on. Not the climbing, they won't replace that soon, but the dispatchers, the planners, the folks in the office who've kept us safe for years. And once they're gone, the thing telling me which line is dead is a program I can't argue with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push for a clause in the 2028 contract: no lay-offs because of new technology, and any tool that touches switching orders gets checked by a person. I'd keep saving, maybe bump it up a little, and I'd make sure Kofi and the young ones get the training money, not just the managers. I wouldn't learn the stuff myself unless they forced me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like hearing a noise in the house at night and not knowing yet if it's the cat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in the office would you worry about first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marguerite in dispatch. She's been on the night desk twenty-two years and she knows every feeder by its nickname. If a program replaces Marguerite, I'd want it to know that 'the long one past the quarry' means Feeder 14.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't learn it unless forced. What if it's in your bucket truck in two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd learn the minimum and grumble the whole way. I know that sounds stubborn. My wife says I took three years to stop using a paper map, and she's right, but I still found every house.

S1.say: The union needs a seat at the table, full stop, and nobody loses a job over a computer. I'd put that in the local newsletter word for word.
S1.think: It worries me more than I let on, mostly for the dispatchers and planners. Once they're gone, the call on which line is dead comes from a program I can't argue with.
S1.do: Pushes for a no-lay-off and human-check clause in the 2028 contract and steers training money to apprentices. Saves a little more each month and avoids learning the tools himself unless required.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like an unexplained noise in the house at night.
S1.quote: If a program replaces Marguerite, I'd want it to know that 'the long one past the quarry' means Feeder 14.
S1.fieldNote: Safety, not pay, is the real heart of Tomas's worry: switching orders decided by software. He is protective of others more than himself. There's a clear tension between fighting for training for apprentices and refusing it for himself, which he admits with some humour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a disaster made by a handful of tech companies, and the government let it happen. I'd be on the picket line or at the town hall, wherever there's a meeting. Online I'd share every story about a robot dropping a line on somebody.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, two years is nothing. A robot that can climb and splice and do it cheaper means the company won't need eleven crews in Eastgate, they'll need three, and the senior ones are expensive. I've got savings, more than most, but savings buy you a year or two, not a career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd call an emergency meeting of the local and get every lineworker in the region talking. I'd stop any extra payments on the mortgage and keep that money liquid, and Efua and I would freeze the kitchen redo we've been saving for. Once it arrives, I'd fight for the longest severance and retraining deal we can get, and I'd hang on to my job as long as they let me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. Like the ground went out from under the ladder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your boys that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them the truth, because they'd see it on the news anyway. I'd say Dad's still got work for now, and the money's fine for a while, and that we'd figure it out together. My older one would ask if the robot gets my hard hat, and I don't know what I'd say to that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said savings buy a year or two. What gets cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The kitchen first, then the summer trip to Efua's mother. Football club fees stay, that's the one thing the boys look forward to all week. After that it's eating into the savings, and I'd hate every withdrawal.

S2.say: This is a disaster made by a handful of tech companies, and the government let it happen. I'd be at every picket line and town hall, and I'd share every story of a robot getting it wrong.
S2.think: Two years is nothing, and the company would go from eleven crews to three, with the expensive senior ones first. My savings buy us a year or two, not a career.
S2.do: Calls an emergency union meeting in the first month and organises across the region. Stops overpaying the mortgage and freezes the kitchen renovation to keep cash on hand, then fights for severance and retraining while holding on to his job.
S2.feel: Sick, as if the ground dropped away under his ladder.
S2.quote: My older one would ask if the robot gets my hard hat, and I don't know what I'd say to that.
S2.fieldNote: This is where Tomas moves from shop-floor scepticism to real fear. He blames tech companies and government in the same breath, and organising is his first instinct. His strong savings calm him for the family but not for his sense of who he is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I said about the fast one, but louder, because now there's time to do something. Five years is a full contract cycle and an election. I'd be telling people to vote and organise like their jobs depend on it, because they do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it's a bit better than two years, but not much. I'd be forty-eight when it lands, too young to retire and too old to start from scratch. The extra time mainly gives me time to fight, not time to change, because I'm not going to turn into a programmer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd push the union to get transition money written into the contract and lobby the council for a public jobs guarantee on the grid. Efua and I would pay down the mortgage harder so it's smaller when it hits. I'd keep climbing and hope the robots take longer on old wooden poles than the companies say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with something to do. That's easier than the fast one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'too young to retire and too old to start from scratch.' What does forty-eight look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Forty-eight is the boys at fourteen and eleven, still years of school, and the mortgage maybe a third left. Forty-eight is when I'd finally be good enough to teach this job properly, and nobody would want it taught.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the union fight doesn't work, then what?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd take whatever's left that still needs hands. Maybe tree crews, maybe storm work, the stuff that's too messy for a robot at first. I genuinely don't have a plan B past that, and I know that's a weakness.

S3.say: Five years is a full contract cycle and an election, so vote and organise like your job depends on it, because it does. I'd be saying it louder than with the fast one.
S3.think: The extra time gives me time to fight, not time to change, because I'm not turning into a programmer. At forty-eight I'd be too young to retire and too old to start from scratch.
S3.do: Pushes for transition money in the contract and lobbies the council for a public jobs guarantee on the grid. Pays down the mortgage faster with his wife and keeps working.
S3.feel: Anxious, but steadier than with two years because there's a fight to put energy into.
S3.quote: Forty-eight is when I'd finally be good enough to teach this job properly, and nobody would want it taught.
S3.fieldNote: The extra three years change Tomas's tactics but not his stance; he uses time for politics, not retraining. His 'too young, too old' line captures a mid-career trap. When pushed on a plan B, he goes quiet before landing on the union again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this properly, so there's no excuse for anyone being left behind. If companies want to bring robots onto the poles, they pay into a fund for every worker they replace. I'd say that at every union meeting for ten years if I had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the ten years scares me in a different way, because people get lazy with time. Everyone, me included, will say there's plenty of time and then it's 2034. I'd be fifty-three when it comes, and that's close enough to pension age that the union could maybe bridge the gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working, keep saving, and in the first year I'd sit down with the pension people and see what fifty-five looks like. I'd push the union for an early-retirement bridge for older lineworkers and real apprenticeships in whatever comes next for the young ones. And maybe, if Efua nags hard enough, I'd let Kofi show me what these tools actually do, just so I'm not caught out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy turning anxious. Less fear, more of a slow weight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people get lazy with time. What would stop you getting lazy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Efua. She'll ask every New Year what we've done about it, and she won't take 'the union's on it' as an answer. And the pension statement every spring, that's a hard number staring at you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your boys would be about twenty-one and eighteen in 2036. What would you tell them about this trade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them don't follow me up the pole just because I did. My dad told me the grid would always need men like him, and he was right for forty years; I can't promise them that.

S4.say: Ten years is enough time to do this properly, so there's no excuse for leaving anyone behind. Any company putting robots on the poles pays into a fund for every worker it replaces.
S4.think: People get lazy with time, me included, and then suddenly it's 2034. At fifty-three I'd be close enough to my pension that a union deal could maybe bridge the gap.
S4.do: Keeps working and saving, and in the first year asks the pension office what retiring at fifty-five would look like. Pushes the union for an early-retirement bridge for older workers and apprenticeships for the young, and may let his apprentice show him the tools.
S4.feel: A slow weight rather than fear, uneasy shading into anxious.
S4.quote: My dad told me the grid would always need men like him, and he was right for forty years; I can't promise them that.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Tomas's thinking turns to his pension and to his sons' choices. He is honest that time can make people complacent, including himself. The small concession of letting his apprentice teach him is the first sign of movement on technology in the whole interview.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, AGI by 2028, no contest. Two years means there's no time to win anything, you just lose quietly. What would help is a law that says a company can't swap people for robots without paying for their retraining and keeping wages for a couple of years, and a union strong enough to make it stick.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about safety, and that's the bit people forget. Every rule on a line crew was written by somebody who got hurt, and I'd want to know who writes the rules for the robot. If something goes wrong on a live line, I want a person to answer for it.

headlineQuote: Every rule on a line crew was written by somebody who got hurt, and I'd want to know who writes the rules for the robot.
portrait: Tomas Mensah is a 43-year-old distribution crew lead and union shop steward at a city electric company's Eastgate yard, with a school-nurse wife, two young sons and a half-paid mortgage. He's proud, funny and stubborn about technology, and he doesn't use AI tools at all. He shrugs off the hype scenario, worries mostly for dispatchers and safety in the gradual one, and becomes alarmed when AGI arrives in two years. With more warning, he uses the time to organise and to plan his pension rather than to retrain. He blames tech firms and a lax government, and he trusts his union more than any employer.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because two years leaves no time to win anything and workers would just lose quietly.
whatWouldHelp: A law making companies pay for retraining and keep wages for a couple of years before replacing people with robots, backed by a union strong enough to enforce it.
